html:
Fine-tuning an AI on your own data can make it leak that data; QR-code phishing; the cybersecurity radar.
TECH RADAR
Tailoring an AI to your company's data can make it leak that data
No. 15 · Thursday 5 November 2026 · Cybersecurity · 6 min read
 
IN 30 SECONDS
1At TU Delft, adapting a code-writing AI to a new dataset cut how much of its original training data could be extracted from 54.9% to 23.5%, but made the new, often private, data easier to pull out.
2Fake QR codes that lead to phishing sites ('quishing') need checking of both the image and the web address together, a Chinese team argues, and builds a model that does it.
3Cybersecurity radar: attacks on AI remain the fastest-growing research topic, and new GitHub projects on prompt injection grew almost twelvefold in a year.
444
new cybersecurity papers today
54.9% → 23.5%
share of original training data extractable before and after fine-tuning
+1,072%
new GitHub projects on prompt injection, Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025
SIGNAL OF THE DAY
The more you fine-tune an AI, the more it spills your data
Empirical Software Engineering · 3 November · Free PDF  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Fabio Salerno, Ali Al-Kaswan, Maliheh Izadi · Delft University of Technology (Netherlands)
Context. AI models can memorise pieces of the data they were trained on, and an attacker can sometimes get them to repeat it word for word. Companies often take a public model and 'fine-tune' it, training it a little more on their own data, which may include proprietary code or sensitive information.
The team built a test to measure how much training data can be extracted from AI models that write code, before and after fine-tuning. Fine-tuning reduces leaks of the original training data, from 54.9% to 23.5% extractable, but the newly added data becomes vulnerable, and smaller models leak it the most. Compressing the model heavily lowers overall memorisation but makes the fine-tuning data relatively more exposed, while lighter fine-tuning methods, which adjust only part of the model, memorise less of it. It is today's signal because many organisations adapt AI models to their internal data: the study shows that this step creates a new privacy risk, and points to ways of reducing it.
PAPERS OF THE DAY · CYBERSECURITY
Spam and phishing detectionstrong growth
Research share +80% in 3 years · 2,319 papers in 2025
What it is about. Phishing tricks people into visiting fake sites that steal passwords or payments. 'Quishing' hides the link inside a QR code, on a parking meter or in an email, so the user cannot read the address before opening it.
A Quishing Detection Model via Global Attention-Based Adaptive Fusion of QR Code and URL Text
ACM Transactions on Internet Technology · 3 November  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Erzhou Zhu and 3 others · Anhui University of Technology, Anhui University (China) · among the authors Hong Zhong, h-index 54
WHAT THEY DOA detector that looks at both the QR code image and the web address it contains, and learns case by case which of the two to trust more, instead of checking them separately.
WHY IT MATTERSQR codes are everywhere, from menus to parking meters: checking image and link together is a step towards phone cameras that warn before opening a fake site. The abstract gives no accuracy figures.
Infrastructure resiliencegrowing
Research share +17% in 3 years · 1,339 papers in 2025
What it is about. Much of the world's oil passes through a few narrow sea passages, such as straits and canals. Wars, accidents or extreme weather can close them, with effects on energy prices everywhere.
Resilience assessment for China's crude oil shipping network considering maritime chokepoint disruptions
Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review · 1 November  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Hanwen Fan and 4 others · Liverpool John Moores University (United Kingdom), Dalian Maritime University (China), Norwegian School of Economics (Norway) · among the authors Zaili Yang, h-index 75
WHAT THEY DOUsing real tanker routes tracked by ship transponders, they model China's crude oil import network, look for the sequence of blocked passages that would hurt it most, and work out the best order to restore them.
RESULTThe damage during recovery does not grow in proportion to how much alternative capacity a blocked passage has, and when key passages close, re-routing ships is not always better than focusing on reopening them.
WHY IT MATTERSA tool for shipping companies and governments to plan for the next blocked strait, rather than reacting after it closes.
Detecting manipulated mediastrong growth
Research share +86% in 3 years · 1,949 papers in 2025
What it is about. Deepfakes are fake videos, photos or voices made with AI. Beyond political misinformation and fraud, they now reach medicine, where manipulated scans could mislead a diagnosis.
Building the trust: AI-based systematic literature review of deepfake detection across modalities and domains
Artificial Intelligence Review · 3 November  Review  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Nitesh Budhwar and 5 others · Maharshi Dayanand University, Koneru Lakshmaiah Education Foundation, ICFAI Foundation for Higher Education (India) · among the authors Yogesh Kumar Sharma, h-index 34
WHAT THEY DOA systematic review of 142 studies on how deepfakes are made and detected, across images, video, audio and medical imaging.
WHY IT MATTERSA map of a fast-moving field, useful for anyone choosing detection tools; it highlights medical deepfakes as an emerging risk.
RADAR OF THE DAY · CYBERSECURITY
What it is about. Protecting computers, networks and data from attacks: from phishing and ransomware to attacks on AI systems themselves, such as prompt injection, hidden instructions that trick a chatbot or an AI agent into doing something it should not.

research share compared with 3 years ago
+24%

Where research is growing (topic share, 2022→2025)
Attacks on AI and how to resist them
making AI models hard to fool; it accelerates most this year
▲ +100%
Detecting manipulated media

▲ +86%
Network security and intrusion detection
alarms that spot attacks in network traffic
▲ +80%
Spam and phishing detection
filtering fraudulent emails, messages and QR codes
▲ +80%
Privacy-preserving technologies
using personal data without exposing people
▲ +77%
What developers and the public do
SIGNALGITHUB
(year on year)		HACKER NEWS
(year on year)
«prompt injection»▲ +1,072%■ +2%
«llm security»▲ +681%▼ −9%
GitHub: new projects; Hacker News: stories discussed (91 and 65 in the quarter). Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025; for comparison, all new GitHub projects grew 62% and Hacker News discussions fell 38%. Wikipedia, 12 months: views up for prompt injection (+42%), down for ransomware (−18%) and post-quantum cryptography (−18%). Adoption data cover only AI-related security; data updated 3 November.
In short: The security of AI itself is the fastest-moving front in research, code and public interest, as today's signal on data leaks from fine-tuned models shows. Classic threats such as ransomware draw less attention than a year ago.
WORDS OF THE DAY
h-index — a measure of how often a researcher is cited: an h-index of 50 means 50 papers cited at least 50 times each. Above 40 usually indicates an established name in the field.
Fine-tuning — training an existing AI model a little more on a smaller, specific dataset, like giving a general doctor a short course in one speciality.
Quishing — phishing through a QR code: scanning it leads to a fake website that tries to steal passwords or money.
Chokepoint — a narrow sea passage, such as a strait or canal, through which a large share of shipping must pass.
WORTH WATCHING
Tomorrow the radar of the day is on robotics and automation. Worth watching: guidance for companies on how to fine-tune AI models on internal data without exposing it.
